Flare Fuzz - Scientific Model-Orchestrated Intelligence System for the Flame in freefall NASA study

FlareFuzz is an open-source scientific data processing and analysis platform designed to help researchers transform complex experimental datasets into structured, comparable and reproducible results.

Built with Python, FastAPI, Pandas, Pydantic, and React, the platform provides dataset ingestion, validation, unit normalization, quality assessment, scientific model fitting, and investigation management through an accessible web interface.

The project addresses the challenge of fragmented scientific workflows, where inconsistent formats, measurement units, and processing methods make experimental results difficult to compare and interpret. FlareFuzz brings these operations together in a unified, API-driven workflow that supports traceability and scientific transparency.

Initially developed with NASA scientific datasets in mind, FlareFuzz aims to reduce repetitive data preparation, improve research accessibility, and establish a foundation for more advanced scientific analysis and collaboration.

Released under the Apache 2.0 license, the project encourages open innovation and further development by the scientific and developer communities.
details:
FlareFuzz — Reproducible Scientific Data Analysis

Project Overview

FlareFuzz is an open-source scientific data processing and analysis platform designed to make experimental datasets easier to ingest, validate, standardize, investigate, and interpret.

The project was developed with NASA scientific research datasets in mind, particularly experiments where inconsistent measurements, fragmented data sources, and uncertainty can complicate scientific analysis.

What Does It Do?

FlareFuzz provides an API-driven workflow for:

  • Ingesting scientific datasets.
  • Validating data structures and measurement values.
  • Normalizing measurements into consistent units.
  • Assessing dataset quality.
  • Organizing scientific investigations.
  • Supporting scientific model fitting and analysis.
  • Exposing processing capabilities through documented API endpoints.

The platform aims to make scientific workflows more transparent and reproducible.

What Does It Not Do?

FlareFuzz does not replace scientific expertise, laboratory experiments, or independent validation of research findings.

It is not a general-purpose AI system that automatically discovers scientific laws. Its purpose is to provide a structured foundation for data processing and analysis.

The current version is a developing research prototype rather than a fully validated production scientific platform.

How Does It Work?

FlareFuzz uses a Python backend built with FastAPI. Incoming data is processed through structured validation and transformation workflows.

Pydantic supports data validation, Pandas handles tabular processing, and Pint provides measurement-unit conversions.

The API exposes operations for dataset ingestion, quality assessment, normalization, investigations, and model fitting. A React-based frontend is being prepared to make these capabilities accessible through a visual interface.

The backend has been deployed to Render, with interactive API documentation available through FastAPI's Swagger interface.

The React front end is reachable at https://mistily.github.io/flarefuzz/ , also hosted as open-source at https://github.com/mistily/flarefuzz

The FastAPI backend is hosted at https://flarefuzz-api.onrender.com/ , also hosted as open-source at https://github.com/mistily/flarefuzz-api

Benefits and Intended Impact

Scientific datasets frequently require extensive preprocessing before researchers can compare measurements or apply analytical models.

FlareFuzz aims to reduce repetitive preparation work, improve consistency, and make data transformations easier to inspect.

Its intended impact is to help researchers, students, and developers build more accessible and reproducible scientific workflows, particularly in interdisciplinary research where datasets use different measurement conventions.

Technologies and Tools

Backend: Python, FastAPI, Pandas, Pydantic, Pint, HTTPX, Uvicorn, and Python Multipart.

Frontend: React, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Vite.

Development and deployment: Git, GitHub, Render, and FastAPI's OpenAPI/Swagger documentation.

Hardware: Conventional development hardware and cloud-hosted CPU resources. No specialized laboratory hardware or GPU is required for the demonstrated API deployment.

License: Apache License 2.0.

Development Approach

The project was developed incrementally, beginning with the scientific data-processing requirements and translating them into modular API operations.

The backend architecture separates data ingestion, validation, normalization, and analytical functionality to support testing and future extension.

Deployment testing helped identify and resolve configuration issues, establish a working public API, and verify that the application's endpoints were accessible.

The React frontend is being integrated as the next stage of development.

What Makes FlareFuzz Creative?

FlareFuzz combines scientific data engineering with an accessible, reusable application architecture.

Rather than treating data cleaning, unit conversion, quality assessment, and scientific modeling as disconnected tasks, the project brings them into a common workflow.

Its creative direction is to make scientific processing more understandable and approachable while preserving the structured operations required for reproducible research.

Team Considerations

During development, the project prioritized:

  • Scientific consistency: Handling measurements and units systematically.
  • Reproducibility: Making processing steps explicit and inspectable.
  • Modularity: Keeping individual processing functions maintainable and extensible.
  • Accessibility: Providing documented APIs and developing a visual frontend.
  • Resource efficiency: Supporting lightweight deployment without specialized computing infrastructure.
  • Openness: Using an open-source license to encourage collaboration and reuse.

Future Development

Planned improvements include completing the frontend deployment and integration, expanding scientific analysis capabilities, improving provenance and uncertainty reporting, and validating workflows against additional experimental datasets.

The long-term vision is an extensible platform that helps turn fragmented scientific data into more consistent, understandable, and reusable research resources.
